title: Right Triangles & Pythagorean Theorem
coreInsight: In a right triangle, the areas of squares on the legs combine to equal the area of the square on the hypotenuse, yielding a^2 + b^2 = c^2.
targetLearnerRealization: Only in a right triangle, the two leg-square areas exactly fill the hypotenuse square; the equation relates areas first and side lengths after taking a root.
learningObjectives: Identify the hypotenuse as the side opposite the right angle in any orientation.
Explain a² + b² = c² as an area relationship.
Use the theorem only when a right angle is established.
Take a square root after solving for a squared side length.
Create right triangles from displacement, altitude, or coordinate change.

continuity.openingCallback: Lock one triangle angle at 90° and identify the opposite side before comparing side lengths.
closingSeeds: Horizontal and vertical coordinate changes create right-triangle distances.
Special right-triangle ratios can replace repeated square calculations.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: The Pythagorean theorem applies to every triangle.
The hypotenuse is the visually longest-looking side rather than the side opposite the right angle.
After finding c² the square root step can be omitted.
The theorem is a distance formula with no area meaning.

beats.purpose: Create the theorem as an area invariant before presenting its equation.
beats.expectedRealization: On a 3-4 right triangle, the 9 and 16 unit squares on the legs exactly account for the 25-square hypotenuse region.
beats.transitionIn: A right angle fixes one corner of a triangle. Build an outward square on each of its three sides and compare coverage.
beats.whyNow: The unit-square areas make the relationship inspectable before symbolic compression.
beats.entryBridge: Add the two leg-square areas, not the leg lengths.
beats.exitBridge: Nine plus sixteen unit squares fill twenty-five unit squares on the opposite side.
learnerPrompts: How many unit squares lie on the two sides meeting at the right angle?
What area must the square on the opposite side have?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The two leg squares contribute 9 + 16 = 25 square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Combine the areas 3² and 4²; do not add the side lengths 3 and 4.

visual.ariaLabel: Squares of areas nine and sixteen combining into a square of area twenty-five around a right triangle

steps.title: Count coverage
steps.body: The leg squares have areas 3² = 9 and 4² = 16.

steps.title: Combine without overlap
steps.body: A valid dissection rearranges those 25 unit squares to fill the square on the opposite side.

resolution.takeaway: For a right triangle, the two leg-square areas equal the hypotenuse-square area.

beats.purpose: Separate a square's area from its side length and require the inverse root.
beats.expectedRealization: An area of 25 means the corresponding side length is sqrt(25)=5, not 25.
beats.transitionIn: The opposite square has area 25. The triangle uses that square's side, not its area.
beats.prompt: If the square built on the unknown side has area 25 square units, what is the side length?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The side length is sqrt(25) = 5.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find the nonnegative number whose square is 25.

steps.title: Reverse the square
steps.body: A side s creates area s². Since s² = 25, s = sqrt(25) = 5.

resolution.takeaway: A squared length is an area; take a root to recover the length.

beats.purpose: Make the right-angle condition explicit before symbolic use.
beats.expectedRealization: The area identity is guaranteed only for a right triangle.
beats.transitionIn: The 3-4-5 dissection used a square corner between the two legs. Remove that condition.
beats.prompt: A triangle has side lengths a, b, and c, with c the longest. What fact is required before writing a² + b² = c²?

options.text: The sketch makes c look horizontal.
c is merely the longest side.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The theorem requires a right angle opposite the hypotenuse.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Being longest is necessary for the hypotenuse but does not prove the triangle is right.

steps.body: In a non-right triangle, the square on the longest side need not equal the sum of the other two square areas. The 90° condition creates the exact identity.

resolution.takeaway: Verify the right angle before using the Pythagorean theorem.

beats.purpose: Identify the hypotenuse structurally across orientation changes.
beats.expectedRealization: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and never one of the two sides forming it.
beats.transitionIn: Rotate the right triangle until no side looks like a familiar base.
beats.prompt: A right-angle marker sits at vertex Q of triangle PQR. Which side is the hypotenuse?

options.text: It depends on the drawing's orientation.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. PR is opposite Q, the right-angle vertex.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The two sides touching Q are the legs; the remaining side is the hypotenuse.

steps.body: PQ and QR form the right angle, so they are legs. PR lies across from that angle and is the hypotenuse.

resolution.takeaway: Find the right angle first; look across for the hypotenuse.

beats.purpose: Compress the discovered area relationship into the theorem after conditions and roles are clear.
beats.expectedRealization: The symbols label two legs and the opposite hypotenuse, not arbitrary side order.
beats.name: Pythagorean theorem
beats.conciseDefinition: In a right triangle, if a and b are the legs forming the right angle and c is the opposite hypotenuse, then the area of the c-square equals the sum of the leg-square areas.
beats.formalization: a² + b² = c² · c = sqrt(a² + b²) · a = sqrt(c² − b²)
beats.memoryHook: Right angle first; legs add as squares; root returns length.

beats.purpose: Turn a multi-segment walk into perpendicular net displacement and a right-triangle distance.
beats.expectedRealization: The two south legs combine to 1 mile, perpendicular to the 3/4-mile east leg, and direct distance is the hypotenuse 5/4.
beats.transitionIn: A right triangle may be hidden inside a route. Collapse movements in the same direction before drawing the direct line.
beats.whyNow: The learner can identify leg directions and recover hypotenuse length from square areas.
beats.entryBridge: Combine the southward motion, keep the eastward motion separate, then connect start to finish.
beats.exitBridge: Perpendicular displacements 1 and 3/4 form a scaled 3-4-5 triangle with hypotenuse 5/4.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A square grid with perpendicular legs and a direct diagonal.
learnerPrompts: What is his total southward displacement?
Which two perpendicular legs connect the same start and finish?
Why is the direct line the hypotenuse, and what is its length?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The direct distance is 5/4 = 1 1/4 miles.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Combine the two south legs into 1 mile, then use that perpendicular to the 3/4-mile east leg.

steps.title: Combine like directions
steps.body: One-half mile south plus another one-half mile south gives 1 mile south; eastward displacement is 3/4 mile.

steps.title: Identify the hypotenuse
steps.body: South and east are perpendicular, so the direct start-to-finish segment lies opposite their right angle.

steps.title: Find the distance
steps.body: 1² + (3/4)² = 1 + 9/16 = 25/16, so the distance is sqrt(25/16) = 5/4 = 1 1/4 miles.

resolution.takeaway: Net perpendicular displacement creates the legs; the direct distance is the hypotenuse.

beats.purpose: Coordinate triangle area, isosceles symmetry, and Pythagorean theorem in a layered solution.
beats.expectedRealization: Area gives altitude 5, symmetry halves the base to 12, and the congruent side is the 13-unit hypotenuse.
beats.transitionIn: The walk supplied both legs directly. In an isosceles triangle, build the right triangle by finding its altitude and half-base.
beats.whyNow: This transfer naturally combines the learner's area, triangle-property, exponent, root, and right-triangle knowledge.
beats.entryBridge: Use area to find height, use isosceles symmetry to bisect the base, then identify the requested side.
beats.exitBridge: The requested equal side is not the height 5; it is the hypotenuse of a 5-12-13 triangle.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A triangle split by a perpendicular altitude into two matching right triangles.
learnerPrompts: What quantities are given and requested?
What height produces area 60 over base 24?
Why is height 5 not the requested side?
How does the altitude split the base?
Which side is the hypotenuse of the 5-by-12 right triangle?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The congruent side is sqrt(5² + 12²) = 13.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find height 5, halve the base to 12, then use the requested slanted side as the hypotenuse.

steps.title: Use symmetry
steps.body: In an isosceles triangle, the altitude from the vertex bisects the 24-unit base into two 12-unit segments.

steps.title: Find the requested side
steps.body: The congruent side is opposite the right angle in a smaller triangle: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169, so its length is sqrt(169) = 13.

resolution.takeaway: Intermediate values have roles: height and half-base are legs; the requested equal side is their hypotenuse.

beats.purpose: Assess direct hypotenuse calculation with the root step.
beats.whyNow: Return to a bare right triangle after two contexts.
beats.entryBridge: Square the legs, add areas, then take the root.
beats.exitBridge: Six and eight produce hypotenuse ten.
learnerPrompts: What value is c², and what length has that square?
beats.incorrectFeedback: After 6² + 8², take the nonnegative square root to get a length.

resolution.takeaway: The sum gives a square area; the root gives the side length.

beats.purpose: Assess subtracting square areas and recovering a leg length.
beats.whyNow: Reverse the theorem with the hypotenuse known.
beats.entryBridge: Subtract the known leg square from the hypotenuse square.
beats.exitBridge: The missing square area is 144, so the leg is 12.
learnerPrompts: Which square area is the total, and which is removed?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use x² + 5² = 13², then take the root after finding x².

resolution.takeaway: To find a leg, subtract square areas before taking a root.

beats.purpose: Assess refusal to apply the theorem without a right-angle condition.
beats.entryBridge: Audit the angle information before using side squares.
beats.exitBridge: Two side lengths alone do not determine the third.
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Without an included angle or another constraint, the third side is not determined.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The formula a² + b² = c² is not authorized unless the triangle is right.

steps.body: Sides 7 and 9 can meet at many angles, producing different third sides. No right angle is given, so Pythagorean equality cannot be assumed.

beats.purpose: Assess horizontal and vertical changes as right-triangle legs.
beats.whyNow: Transfer the walking model to coordinates.
beats.entryBridge: Find absolute horizontal and vertical changes, not endpoint coordinates themselves.
learnerPrompts: What are the two perpendicular coordinate changes?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The points are 15 units apart.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use horizontal change 9 and vertical change 12 as the legs.

steps.body: The changes are |11 − 2| = 9 and |13 − 1| = 12. Distance = sqrt(9² + 12²) = sqrt(225) = 15.

beats.purpose: Assess creating a right triangle inside a rectangle and using area afterward.
beats.whyNow: Finish with a diagonal used as an intermediate dimension.
beats.entryBridge: The rectangle's sides are perpendicular legs of the diagonal triangle.
beats.exitBridge: The diagonal is 15, giving square area 225.
learnerPrompts: Which right triangle supplies the square's side length?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The diagonal is 15, so the constructed square has area 225.
beats.incorrectFeedback: First find the rectangle diagonal from legs 9 and 12, then square that length for the new area.

steps.title: Use it as a new side
steps.body: A square built on that diagonal has area d² = 225 square units.

resolution.takeaway: Track whether a squared value is an area or an intermediate step toward length.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the theorem's condition, roles, area meaning, and root step.
beats.expectedRealization: Reliable use begins with structure and ends with dimensional interpretation.
beats.transitionIn: Side-squares, walking routes, altitudes, coordinates, and diagonals all used one area identity inside a verified right triangle.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable Pythagorean routine? Select all four.

options.text: Verify or construct a right angle.
Identify the two legs and the opposite hypotenuse.
Add leg-square areas or subtract from the hypotenuse-square area.
Take a nonnegative square root when the question asks for length.

response.feedback: Each action protects one part of the theorem's meaning.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Right angle, side roles, square areas, then the root when length is needed.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four are essential; skipping one changes the mathematical claim.

visual.ariaLabel: A right-triangle checklist connecting the right angle, side roles, square areas, and square root

steps.body: The theorem is an area equation with a geometric condition. Algebra then isolates a square, and a root converts that area value back to a side length.

resolution.takeaway: Right angle first; square areas next; length last.

beats.purpose: Consolidate transfer to grid and coordinate distance without claiming a curriculum successor.
beats.expectedRealization: Many direct distances are hypotenuses once perpendicular changes are exposed.
beats.transitionIn: A winding route and two coordinate points both hid the same pair of perpendicular changes.
beats.prompt: When a direct distance is hard to measure, how can horizontal and vertical changes turn it into a right-triangle problem?
beats.takeaway: Expose perpendicular components, then let their square areas determine the direct distance.

notes: Design: unit-square areas on a 3-4-5 right triangle establish the theorem before notation. A separate step reverses square area to side length, followed by explicit gates for the right-angle condition and hypotenuse identification. Authentic problems create right triangles from net displacement and an isosceles altitude.

Beat outline: side-square anchor -> area-to-length -> right-angle gate -> hypotenuse roles -> name theorem -> authentic walk -> authentic isosceles transfer -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> distance reflection.
Both mapped animations are referenced unchanged after submission over their full declared timelines. Existing choice-grid visuals suffice; no renderer or animation source changes were made.

Generated answers were recomputed through square-area sums or differences and roots, with independent Pythagorean triples, coordinate reconstruction, condition counterexamples, or area reversal audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
